lmsArticle.title: System Design HLD Example: Hotel Booking System (Airbnb)
lmsArticle.subtitle: A senior-level HLD for a hotel booking platform handling availability, concurrency, and reservations.
lmsArticle.excerpt: A robust hotel booking system must guarantee atomicity in inventory subtraction. The core trade-off is **Consistency vs. Availability**: we prioritize strong consistency for the booking path (PostgreSQL with Optimistic Locking) while allowing eventual consistency and high availability for the search path (Elasticsearch). A two-phase "Hold-then-Confirm" model ensures that inventory isn't leaked during payment failures.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

A robust hotel booking system must guarantee atomicity in inventory subtraction. The core trade-off is **Consistency vs. Availability**: we prioritize strong consistency for the booking path (PostgreSQL with Optimistic Locking) while allowing eventual consistency and high availability for the search path (Elasticsearch). A two-phase "Hold-then-Confirm" model ensures that inventory isn't leaked during payment failure…

This walkthrough focuses on **The New Year's Eve Nightmare**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Imagine it’s 11:59 PM on New Year’s Eve.
- Two different travelers, one in London and one in New York, are looking at the exact same penthouse in Manhattan for the upcoming weekend.
- Both click "Book Now" at the same millisecond.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, sorting-and-searching-algorithms, consistency-replication

## Stage 1 — Global Reservation Systems: Use Cases & Requirements

- Actors - Guest / Traveler: Searches for rooms, views availability, and makes reservations.
- - Host / Property Manager: Manages inventory, sets pricing, and views upcoming bookings.
- - Admin: Handles disputes, refunds, and platform-wide monitoring.
- Functional Requirements - Search: Users can search rooms by location (geo-coordinates), date range, and guest count.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Functional Requirements - Search: Users can search rooms by location (geo-coordinates), date range, and guest count.

## Stage 2 — Basics: Baseline Architecture

- At its core, a booking system is an Inventory Management Engine .
- Unlike a standard e-commerce site where you might have 1,000 units of a SKU, a hotel booking system has "Perishable Inventory." A room night on December 31st is a different "product" than the same room on January 1st.
- The baseline architecture involves: 1.
- Inventory Generation: Pre-calculating available slots for every room for the next 365 days.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

```architecture

  "version": 1,
  "title": "Basics: Baseline Architecture - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant",
    "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers."
  }
}
```

**Observable outcome:** Inventory Generation: Pre-calculating available slots for every room for the next 365 days.

## Stage 3 — Mechanics: Distribution & Processing Logic

- The distribution of inventory must be handled carefully.
- When a host adds a new listing, we don't just add one row.
- We must generate 365 rows in the availability slots table.
- - Inventory Fan-out: Every update to a room's base availability (e.g., taking the room offline for maintenance) must propagate to all 365 days.

*Applies **sorting-and-searching-algorithms** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Inventory Fan-out: Every update to a room's base availability (e.g., taking the room offline for maintenance) must propagate to all 365 days.

## Stage 4 — Estimations & Design Goals

- The Math of Inventory - Total Listings: 10 Million rooms.
- - Booking Window: 1 year (365 days).
- - Total Inventory Rows: 10M 365 = 3.65 Billion rows .
- - Search-to-Booking Ratio: 20:1.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Search-to-Booking Ratio: 20:1.

## Stage 5 — High-Level Design: Separating Search from Booking

- The following architecture ensures that high-volume search traffic never interferes with the critical booking path.
- The diagram captures the defining architectural decision: a hard separation between the Search Path (Elasticsearch + Redis) and the Booking Path (Postgres with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED).
- The CDC pipeline via Debezium keeps the two paths synchronized without coupling them — a booking written to Postgres propagates to Elasticsearch within 1–2 seconds, keeping search results fresh while ensuring the bookin…

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

```architecture

  "version": 1,
  "title": "High-Level Design: Separating Search from Booking - Subsystem Overview",
  "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persistent datastores.",
  "view": "high-level",
  "pattern": "microservices",
  "direction": "LR",
  "groups": [
    { "id": "edge", "label": "Edge Traffic Ingress", "tone": "slate" },
    { "id": "services", "label": "Stateless Microservices", "tone": "blue" },
    { "id": "data", "label": "Datastore Infrastructure", "tone": "green" }
  ],
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "gw", "component": "api-gateway", "label": "API Gateway", "group": "edge", "badge": "TLS & Auth" },
    { "id": "app", "component": "workflow-service", "label": "Domain Service", "group": "services", "badge": "Stateless" },
    { "id": "cache", "component": "redis", "label": "Redis Cache", "group": "data", "badge": "Sub-ms Reads" },
    { "id": "db", "component": "postgres", "label": "Transactional DB", "group": "data", "badge": "ACID Log" }
  ],
  "edges": [
    { "from": "gw", "to": "app", "kind": "request", "label": "gRPC Request" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "cache", "kind": "read", "label": "Cache Lookups" },
    { "from": "app", "to": "db", "kind": "write", "label": "Durable Write" }
  ],
  "takeaway": {
    "title": "Architecture Boundary Invariant",
    "body": "Stateless compute nodes scale horizontally while shielding underlying database clusters behind fast cache layers."
  }

```

```mermaid
graph TD
    User((User)) --> LB[Load Balancer]
    LB --> AG[API Gateway]
    
    subgraph Search_Path
        AG --> SS[Search Service]
        SS --> ES[(Elasticsearch: Geo + Dates)]
        SS --> RC[(Search Cache: Redis)]
    end
    
    subgraph Booking_Path
        AG --> BS[Booking Service]
        BS --> AS[Availability Service]
        AS --> PDB[(Primary DB: Postgres)]
        BS --> PS[Payment Service]
    end
    
    subgraph Async_Sync
        PDB --> CDC[Debezium / CDC]
        CDC --> Kafka[Kafka]
        Kafka --> SS
        Kafka --> NS[Notification Service]
    end
```

**Observable outcome:** The CDC pipeline via Debezium keeps the two paths synchronized without coupling them — a booking written to Postgres propagates to Elasticsearch within 1–2 seconds, keeping search results fresh while ensuring the bookin…

## Stage 6 — Deep Dive: How Postgres Atomically Prevents the Double-Booking Race Condition

- The Hold mechanism is the most critical internal component.
- Understanding exactly how it works at the database level reveals why no amount of application-level locking can replace it — only the database can guarantee atomicity across concurrent transactions.
- Internals: The Hold-then-Confirm State Machine When a guest selects a room and date range, the Booking Service must atomically transition N rows in the availability slots table (one per night) from AVAILABLE to HELD .
- The key word is "atomically": if any single night in the requested range is already HELD or BOOKED by another session, the entire operation must roll back with no writes committed.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** The key word is "atomically": if any single night in the requested range is already HELD or BOOKED by another session, the entire operation must roll back with no writes committed.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- Lesson 1 — The hold is your correctness anchor.
- Every architectural decision should be evaluated against one question: "Does this preserve the integrity of the hold?" Adding a caching layer between the Booking Service and Postgres is dangerous if the cached availabil…

## Alternatives considered

The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here.

## Failure and degraded modes

### Consistency vs. Availability: Trade-offs in the Booking Path

- **Detection:** Critical Failure Mode — The Hold-Expiry and Payment Gap: A guest places a hold, begins payment, and the payment takes 16 minutes (possible with 3D Secure strong authentication).
- **User or operator impact:** Critical Failure Mode — The Hold-Expiry and Payment Gap: A guest places a hold, begins payment, and the payment takes 16 minutes (possible with 3D Secure strong authentication).

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
